lines.text: Why does eating ice cream too fast trigger a stabbing headache behind your eyes?
The medical name is sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia, and your brain isn't actually freezing at all.
When cold slush hits the roof of your mouth, it rapidly cools sensitive blood vessels at the palate.
To protect your brain from temperature shock, these arteries violently constrict and then flood with warm blood.
This sudden surge triggers pain receptors in the trigeminal nerve, which also senses facial pain.
Your brain gets confused by the nerve signals, mistakenly feeling the pain in your forehead and eyes.
To stop it instantly, press your warm tongue flat against the roof of your mouth.
